NLP.overview: Natural Language Processing (NLP) is the field of AI focused on enabling computers to understand, interpret, and generate human language.
NLP.folder_structure:
nlp_project/
  data/
  notebooks/
  src/
    preprocessing.py
    model.py
  requirements.txt
common_errors: Forgetting to lowercase/tokenize text before vectorizing
Using a vocabulary fit on training data but not reused for test data
Ignoring stopword removal leading to noisy features
steps: Collect and clean raw text data
Tokenize and normalize (lowercase, remove punctuation)
Vectorize with TF-IDF or Bag-of-Words
Train a classifier (e.g. Logistic Regression, Naive Bayes)
Evaluate with precision/recall/F1
NLP.detailed_explanation: NLP is the bridge between raw human text and something a machine can compute on. Under the hood, every NLP pipeline does the same three things: turn text into numbers (representation), learn or apply a mapping from those numbers to an output (modeling), and turn the model's output back into something a human understands (interpretation). Classic NLP (TF-IDF + Logistic Regression / Naive Bayes) treats a sentence as a bag of weighted word counts and works well for topic/sentiment classification on modest data. Modern NLP (transformers) instead learns dense contextual embeddings — the vector for 'bank' differs between 'river bank' and 'bank loan' — which is what makes tasks like NER, translation, and summarization possible. As a learner, start with the classic pipeline so you understand *why* vectorization matters, then move to transformer fine-tuning once the fundamentals (tokenization, vectorization, evaluation) are solid.

tasks: Learn what a corpus, token, and vocabulary are, and why raw text can't go into a model directly
Practice tokenization, lowercasing, punctuation/stopword removal with NLTK or spaCy
Implement Bag-of-Words and TF-IDF vectorization from scratch once, then with scikit-learn
Understand precision, recall, F1, and confusion matrices before touching any model
Pick a small labeled dataset (SMS Spam, IMDB Reviews, 20 Newsgroups)
Build train/test split with stratification so class balance is preserved
Train Logistic Regression and Naive Bayes; compare accuracy/F1 side by side
Do error analysis: read 10 misclassified examples and note *why* the model failed
Save the fitted vectorizer + model together (pickle/joblib) so inference reuses the same vocabulary
Learn what word embeddings solve that TF-IDF cannot (semantic similarity, synonyms)
Try a pretrained sentence-embedding model locally to compute text similarity
Fine-tune (or at least run inference with) a small local transformer classifier
Compare transformer results vs your classic baseline on the same test set and dataset split
Wrap the trained pipeline in a simple function/API (input text -> label + confidence)
Add basic input validation (empty text, non-English text, very long text)
Try a second task on the same skills — NER, summarization, or intent classification
Write a short README documenting preprocessing steps so results are reproducible

SLM.overview: Small Language Models (SLMs) are compact transformer models (typically under ~10B parameters) designed to run efficiently on local or edge hardware.
SLM.folder_structure:
slm_project/
  models/
  prompts/
  src/
    inference.py
  requirements.txt
common_errors: Running a model too large for available RAM
Not quantizing the model for local inference
steps: Choose a small model (e.g. phi3:mini, qwen2.5:3b)
Install and run it locally via Ollama or llama.cpp
Design and test prompts
Wrap inference in a local API for your app
Evaluate output quality manually or with a rubric
SLM.detailed_explanation: Small Language Models trade raw capability for something GPT-4-class models can't offer: they run on a laptop or phone, respond in milliseconds instead of seconds, cost nothing per token, and keep every prompt fully offline/private. The core skill isn't training an SLM from scratch (almost nobody does that) — it's *selecting, quantizing, running, and prompting* an existing open-weight model efficiently. A quantized 3-4B model (e.g. Phi-3-mini, Qwen2.5-3B, Gemma-2B) can already do decent summarization, extraction, and simple reasoning if the prompt is well-scoped. The main engineering skill to build is knowing the model's real limits — context window, reasoning depth, hallucination rate — and designing your app around them (shorter prompts, retrieval instead of memorization, structured output formats).

roadmap.phase: Phase 1 — Get a Model Running Locally (Day 1-2)
tasks: Install Ollama (or llama.cpp) and pull a small model such as phi3:mini or qwen2.5:3b
Run a few prompts from the CLI and observe response latency and quality
Learn what quantization (Q4, Q5, Q8) trades off between speed, RAM use, and accuracy
Check your hardware limits: RAM needed roughly scales with model size x quant level
Write 5-10 test prompts representative of your real use case, not toy examples
Compare zero-shot vs few-shot prompting on the same task
Track a simple rubric (correctness, format compliance, hallucination) per response
Identify the model's failure modes: long context loss, math errors, made-up facts

roadmap.phase: Phase 3 — Wrap It in an App (Week 2)
tasks: Build a thin local API/function around ollama's REST endpoint (or Python client)
Add structured output constraints (JSON schema, regex validation, retries on bad output)
Add context-window-aware truncation so long inputs don't silently get cut mid-sentence
Log every prompt/response pair locally for later evaluation
Benchmark 2-3 different small models on the *same* eval set (latency, quality, RAM)
Try a smaller quantization level and measure the quality/speed tradeoff
If quality is insufficient, decide: bigger SLM, RAG (external knowledge), or a cloud model as fallback
Document which model you chose and why, with the numbers to back it

Agentic AI.overview: Agentic AI systems use an LLM (or rules) to plan, take actions via tools, observe results, and iterate toward a goal.
Agentic AI.folder_structure:
agent_project/
  tools/
  memory/
  src/
    planner.py
    executor.py
  requirements.txt
common_errors: No loop termination condition (infinite tool calls)
Not validating tool outputs before reuse
Overloading a single agent with too many responsibilities
steps: Define the agent's goal and available tools
Implement a planning/reasoning step
Implement tool execution with error handling
Add memory/state tracking between steps
Add a stopping condition and test edge cases
Agentic AI.detailed_explanation: An agent is a loop, not a single call: Plan -> Act -> Observe -> Repeat -> Stop. The LLM (or rule-based planner) decides *what tool to use next* based on the goal and what's happened so far, a tool executes and returns a result, the agent observes that result and updates its plan, and the loop continues until a stopping condition is met (goal achieved, max steps hit, or a hard error). The single biggest source of bugs in agent projects is a missing or weak stopping condition — agents that call tools forever, or that never validate a tool's output before acting on it again. The second biggest is giving one agent too many responsibilities; multi-agent designs (a planner agent + specialized worker agents) tend to be more debuggable than one giant agent with 15 tools.

tasks: Write the agent's goal in one sentence, and list every tool it's allowed to use
Draw the Plan -> Act -> Observe -> Stop loop on paper before writing any code
Decide the stopping conditions up front: max iterations, success check, budget/timeout
Decide what 'memory' the agent needs between steps (scratchpad, conversation history, files)
Implement each tool as a pure function with clear inputs/outputs and explicit error returns
Implement the planning step (LLM call or rule-based) that picks the next action
Implement the executor that runs the chosen tool and captures success/failure
Add the stop condition check at the *top* of every loop iteration, not just at the end
Validate every tool output before feeding it back into the next planning step
Add retry logic with a cap (don't retry forever on the same failing tool call)
Log every step (thought, action, observation) so you can replay and debug a run
Test deliberately adversarial cases: a tool that fails, returns garbage, or times out
Split one overloaded agent into a planner + specialized sub-agents if responsibilities have grown
Add a budget (max tool calls or max tokens) to bound worst-case cost/time
Add human-in-the-loop confirmation before any irreversible action (sending, deleting, paying)
Write a small eval set of tasks the agent must complete, and re-run it after every change

Generative AI.overview: Generative AI covers models that create new content (text, images, audio) rather than just classifying or predicting a label.
Generative AI.folder_structure:
genai_project/
  data/
  src/
    generator.py
  outputs/
  requirements.txt
common_errors: Not normalizing input data before training
Evaluating generative quality with the wrong metric
steps: Pick a generative approach (GAN, VAE, or local LLM)
Prepare and normalize training data
Build and train a small model or configure a local model
Generate samples and qualitatively review them
Iterate on architecture or prompts
Generative AI.detailed_explanation: Generative models learn the underlying *distribution* of the training data so they can draw new, plausible samples from it, instead of just mapping an input to a fixed label. A GAN does this adversarially (a generator tries to fool a discriminator); a VAE does it by learning a compressed latent space and decoding samples back out; a local LLM does it autoregressively, predicting the next token given everything before it. The practical skill for a beginner isn't picking the fanciest architecture — it's getting a *small* generative model to train stably on a *small* dataset first (MNIST digits, a tiny text corpus), because failure modes like mode collapse and exploding loss are much easier to diagnose at small scale than after committing days of training time to something large.

roadmap.phase: Phase 1 — Pick an Approach & Prepare Data (Day 1-2)
tasks: Choose GAN, VAE, or a local LLM based on your output type (images vs text) and compute budget
Pick a small, well-understood dataset (MNIST for images, a small text corpus for text)
Normalize/scale input data (e.g. pixel values to [-1, 1] or [0, 1]) before training
Decide your evaluation approach up front — generative quality has no single perfect metric

roadmap.phase: Phase 2 — Build & Train a Small Model (Day 3-7)
tasks: Implement a minimal generator/discriminator (GAN) or encoder/decoder (VAE) — small on purpose
Train for a short run first and sanity-check outputs before scaling up epochs
Watch for mode collapse (GAN outputs becoming near-identical) or posterior collapse (VAE)
Log loss curves for every component (generator loss, discriminator loss, reconstruction loss)
Qualitatively review a grid of generated samples, not just the loss number
Try a quantitative proxy metric where relevant (e.g. FID for images) alongside human review
Tune one hyperparameter at a time (learning rate, latent dim, batch size) and re-check outputs
If using a local LLM instead, evaluate coherence/relevance on held-out prompts
Try conditional generation (class-conditional GAN/VAE, or prompt-conditioned LLM output)
Add basic safety/quality filtering on generated outputs before they reach a user
Package generation behind a simple function/API with clear input constraints
Document known failure modes so future users of your model know its limits

RAG.overview: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) combines a document retriever with a language model so answers are grounded in your own data.
RAG.folder_structure:
rag_project/
  documents/
  src/
    embed.py
    retrieve.py
    generate.py
  index/
  requirements.txt
common_errors: Chunking documents too large or too small
Not normalizing embeddings before similarity search
Feeding irrelevant retrieved chunks into the prompt
steps: Chunk and clean your source documents
Generate embeddings for each chunk locally
Build a vector index (FAISS/Chroma)
Retrieve top-k relevant chunks for a query
Feed retrieved context + query into a local LLM for the answer

Prompt Engineering.overview: Prompt engineering is the practice of designing inputs to a language model to reliably get the desired output.
Prompt Engineering.folder_structure:
prompt_project/
  prompts/
  evaluations/
  src/
    test_prompts.py
  requirements.txt
dataset_suggestions: A small set of representative test queries for your use case
common_errors: Not specifying the desired output format
Testing only one prompt variant instead of comparing several
steps: Define the task and desired output format clearly
Write an initial prompt with explicit instructions
Add few-shot examples if needed
Test against multiple sample inputs
Iterate based on failure cases
